note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

constraints: root is a canonical LeetCode N-ary level-order list
clarifyingQuestions: How is the tree passed: node objects or a serialized list?
Which level wins a tie?
What is returned for an empty tree?
hints: Breadth-first search visits a whole level before the next one.
In the level-order list, each null closes the child group of one node in breadth-first order.
Count the nodes of each level as you walk and keep the first strictly larger count.
invariants: levels are visited in increasing order
the answer only changes on a strictly larger count
tradeoffs: The parse already walks the tree breadth-first, so no node objects are needed
hack2hire:68dc2e1c9736cfa4e906240c.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: widest level of an N-ary tree

constraints: weights: decimals with at most 4 places summing to exactly 1
threshold in [0, 1] with at most 4 decimal places
clarifyingQuestions: How is the similarity of two records computed from the weights?
Do two empty values count as a match?
Is the threshold inclusive?
In which order should pairs be listed?
hints: Decimal weights with at most 4 places become exact integers when scaled by 10000.
Rows that share a value in a field can be found through a hash map from value to rows.
Accumulate each row's scores against later rows in an array, then compare each entry with the threshold.
invariants: every score is an integer count of ten-thousandths
pairs are emitted in row order
chooseWhen: Weighted exact-match deduplication of small tables
tradeoffs: Listing all pairs is quadratic in the worst case; blocking only helps when values are diverse
hack2hire:697c3db29731315964cfb08b.variantLabel: Inferred level 1 of 3: list linked record pairs

constraints: weights: decimals with at most 4 places summing to exactly 1
threshold in [0, 1] with at most 4 decimal places
clarifyingQuestions: Are links transitive?
Should single unlinked records be reported?
How are groups and their members ordered?
hints: Linked records form the edges of a graph; groups are its connected components.
A union-find joins rows as links are found.
Visit rows in order and append each to its root's group so members and groups come out in row order.
invariants: two rows share a root exactly when a chain of links joins them
groups are listed by their first row
chooseWhen: Clustering records by a pairwise match rule
tradeoffs: Union-find needs every linked pair to be found; the pair scan stays quadratic
hack2hire:697d9ce2b8c468a441586158.variantLabel: Inferred level 2 of 3: transitive groups of linked records

constraints: weights: decimals with at most 4 places summing to exactly 1
threshold in [0, 1] with at most 4 decimal places
clarifyingQuestions: Which match is reported when several records tie?
What is reported for a record with no link?
Can a record match itself?
hints: Each row needs its score against every other row.
Scaled integer weights make score comparisons exact.
Scan scores in row order and replace the best only on a strictly larger score so the earliest row wins ties.
invariants: a record never matches itself
the reported match has the largest linked score
chooseWhen: Nearest-neighbour lookup under an additive exact-match score
tradeoffs: Keeping a full score row per record costs O(n) memory at a time instead of O(1)
hack2hire:697da047b8c468a441586160.variantLabel: Inferred level 3 of 3: best linked match per record

constraints: no self edges, no duplicate edges, no cycles
clarifyingQuestions: Does a service split its load among dependencies or send the full load to each?
Should unreachable services be listed?
How should the result be ordered?
hints: The load of a service is the sum of the loads of the services calling it.
Process services in topological order so each load is final before it is passed on.
Kahn's algorithm gives that order with a queue of services whose callers are all done.
invariants: a service leaves the queue only after all its callers
load factors equal path counts from the entry
chooseWhen: Counting paths or propagating flow in a DAG
tradeoffs: Path counts grow exponentially with depth, so exact integers need a bound or big integers
hack2hire:67cf7ef7aca6a2fa74a72d1f.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: path-count load factors in a service DAG

clarifyingQuestions: Which bracket kinds may contain which?
May a bracket contain the same kind?
Is the answer a length or the substring?
hints: The classic stack solution for one bracket kind measures a valid run back to the last unmatched position.
A frame on the stack can also remember the highest rank closed inside it.
A closer that mismatches or would hold a higher rank becomes a barrier: clear the stack there.
invariants: the text after the bottom barrier and each open frame is a valid concatenation
each frame's rank record covers exactly the pairs closed inside it
chooseWhen: Longest well-formed run under nesting constraints
tradeoffs: The interval recursion handles arbitrary grammars but is cubic
hack2hire:6789c01711318cc872dd83ee.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: longest valid substring under ranked nesting

constraints: rows have equal length and contain only U P . X
clarifyingQuestions: Is the exit any border cell or a marked cell?
Who moves first in a minute, you or the threat?
Can you share a cell with the threat at the moment it arrives?
Does a border start count as escaped?
hints: Threat arrival times do not depend on your moves.
One multi-source BFS from every P gives each cell's threat time.
A second BFS from U may enter a cell only if it arrives strictly before the threat.
invariants: BFS arrival minutes are the earliest possible
a visited cell was safe on arrival
chooseWhen: Shortest escape under time-dependent blocking that spreads at the same speed
tradeoffs: Precomputing threat times costs a full grid pass even when the exit is near
hack2hire:6866f15ea2d59460201f2c7e.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: reach the border ahead of a spreading threat

clarifyingQuestions: How are the states encoded?
Is the answer the length of the run or the flips used?
Can a flip cover servers that are already ON?
hints: Flipping ON servers off never helps.
Each operation can turn at most one maximal block of OFF servers inside the final run into ON.
So find the longest window containing at most k zero blocks with a sliding window.
invariants: the window holds at most k zero blocks
blocks are counted where they start inside the window
chooseWhen: Longest segment with at most k "bad" groups
tradeoffs: Counting blocks instead of zeros needs care when the left edge cuts a block
hack2hire:67800c576fee41e51af73dd8.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: longest ON run after at most k range flips

clarifyingQuestions: Can you fly with 0 energy?
Does resting at full energy do anything?
Is the answer the total distance?
hints: The state after each day is just the remaining energy.
Keep the best distance for each energy level.
With k >= n you can fly every day.
invariants: dp[e] is the best distance with exactly e energy after the processed days
energy stays within 0..k
chooseWhen: Resource-limited choices with a small resource range
tradeoffs: O(n * k) is only practical for small k; the bound n * k <= 1e6 is inferred
hack2hire:67fd5511d2adf72ba62b0ec8.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: maximise distance with capped energy

clarifyingQuestions: Can layers be negative?
What is returned: every start's score or the best one?
Does a failed level consume energy?
hints: Remaining energy after level j from start i is K minus a range sum of layers.
Rewrite the pass test as prefix[j + 1] + energy[j] <= K + prefix[i].
The right side grows with i, so the first failing level can be tracked with a pointer that only moves right.
invariants: all levels between the start and the pointer pass
the pointer never moves left
chooseWhen: Per-start runs with a monotone threshold
tradeoffs: Negative layer values would break the monotone pointer
hack2hire:69efd5e296981f58ae1f6dc7.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: levels passed from every start

clarifyingQuestions: Is the answer the per-node count or the total?
Can a node receive no tasks?
Do all tasks have to be assigned?
hints: Only the count of each type matters.
A type can be used by at most min(count, m) different nodes.
Show that t per node works exactly when the sum of min(count, m) is at least m * t.
invariants: a type contributes at most one task per node
the total is a multiple of m
tradeoffs: The closed form needs a feasibility proof; the flow reference is slower but direct
hack2hire:6a8615b8701a76fc6843aed0.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: equal-size distinct-type assignment

constraints: rows have equal length and contain only P - X
clarifyingQuestions: Can paths pass through X tiles?
Is the answer the tallest building or the whole height map?
What if a building cannot reach any parking lot?

Start one BFS from all P tiles at once.
Any building tile left unvisited has no bound.

clarifyingQuestions: Are the intervals closed or half-open?
Do intervals touching at one point overlap?
What is returned for no intervals?
hints: The best point can always be taken at some interval start.
Sweep sorted starts and ends with a counter.
With closed intervals, process starts before ends at equal coordinates.

constraints: edges [u, v, w]: 0 <= u, v < n, u != v, 0 <= w <= 10, no duplicate (u, v)
clarifyingQuestions: Are multipliers real numbers or integers?
Must the path be simple?
What is returned when end is unreachable or equals start?
hints: Multipliers above 1 make this a longest-path problem, so shortest-path tricks fail.
With few nodes, a simple path is determined by its visited set and last node.
Extend best[mask][v] along every edge v -> w with w not in mask.
invariants: every mask state is a simple path from start
products only grow by multiplying non-negative integers
chooseWhen: Best simple path in a tiny graph
tradeoffs: Exponential in n; usable only for small graphs
hack2hire:67e4468750b60b77022f381c.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: best product over simple paths

clarifyingQuestions: How is the vacation table laid out?
Is the flight count a tie-breaker or a separate objective?
Does flying in week 0 count?
hints: The state each week is just the current city.
Compare plans by days first, then fewer flights.
Flying into c uses the best other city, which is the best or second-best city of the previous week.
invariants: each city's pair is the lexicographic best ending there
the top two previous cities are distinct
chooseWhen: Lexicographic DP with a complete transition graph
tradeoffs: The top-two trick relies on every city being reachable from every other

constraints: dequeue, getMin and getMax only on a non-empty queue
clarifyingQuestions: What are the min and max method names?
What happens on an empty queue?
Is O(1) amortised acceptable?
hints: A deque of candidates can hold the minimum of a sliding window.
Keep the min deque non-decreasing: drop larger back entries before appending.
On dequeue, pop a deque front only if it equals the leaving value.
invariants: the min deque is non-decreasing and its front is the queue minimum
the max deque is non-increasing and its front is the queue maximum
chooseWhen: Sliding-window extremes or queues with range queries
tradeoffs: Amortised O(1); a single enqueue can pop many deque entries
